title: A 1600s puzzle about a blind man gaining sight was tested in 2011
body: William Molyneux sent John Locke a puzzle: a man born blind learns by touch to tell a cube from a sphere; if he were made to see, could he name them by sight alone, before touching them? Locke said no. For centuries the question was all but untestable, because people who gain sight after lifelong blindness are so rare. Then Pawan Sinha’s team at MIT tested five patients, aged 8 to 17, within 48 hours of sight-restoring surgery: at first they matched felt shapes to seen ones **barely better than guessing**, though within days three of them were scoring 80–90 per cent.

slides.text: Suppose a man born blind … taught by his touch to distinguish between a cube and a sphere … the blind man be made to see: whether by his sight, before he touched them, he could now distinguish and tell which is the globe, which the cube?
slides.attribution: William Molyneux, quoted in Locke’s Essay Concerning Human Understanding

steps.label: Born blind, he knows cube and globe by touch
Now imagine he is given sight
Before touching, can he tell which is which?
Locke: no. Leibniz: yes, by reasoning
2011: not at first, but within days

left.label: Locke, Berkeley
left.text: No. Sight and touch are separate; only experience ties a seen shape to a felt one.

right.label: Leibniz
right.text: Yes, with reasoning: both senses share geometry, so he could work out which is which.

slides.heading: The 2011 test
items: Five patients aged 8 to 17 who could only tell light from dark have surgery
Within 48 hours they feel an object, then try to pick it out by sight
Result: matches barely better than chance

slides.label: known cases, by a 1971 estimate, of sight gained after lifelong blindness in 1,000 years
slides.text: That rarity is why Molyneux’s question stayed a thought experiment for so long. His own wife was blind.

slides.question: What did the newly sighted patients do when asked to match a felt shape to a seen one?
options: Failed at first, then learned in days
Never managed it, even after months
slides.explanation: Right after surgery their matches were barely better than chance; three of them, retested days later, reached 80–90 per cent.

slides.heading: Could he name the cube by sight alone? Who said what

items.text: William Molyneux, who posed the question

slides.explanation: Molyneux answered ‘Not’, and Locke and Berkeley agreed; Leibniz argued the man could reason it out, since both senses share geometry.
